summary: Defines MIB objects, in SMIv2 format, for managing source routes on end stations of Token Ring networks where IEEE source routing is used. It is now historic.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 1749 defines a set of management objects for stations on Token Ring networks that use source routing. It lets a network manager read which routes a station has learned, and in principle change them, using the ordinary SNMP management framework. The memo gives the exact structure of the table, the four values in each row, and the rules for what an implementation must support.

what is a routing information field
how do you manage token ring source routes with snmp
subtitle: SNMP objects for reading and managing the source routes a Token Ring station has learned.

tldr.problem: A station on a source-routing Token Ring network keeps a table of the routes it has learned, but there was no standard way for a network manager to see or change that table over SNMP.
tldr.mechanism: The memo defines one table, the 802.5 Station Source Route Table, with four objects per row: the destination MAC address, the Routing Control field, the sequence of bridge and ring identifiers, and the row status. The objects are named in SMIv2 and attached to an interface through the ifIndex value from MIB-II.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1749 is Historic and the RFC Editor recommends it for no further use. It was written as an incremental update to the IEEE 802.5 Token Ring MIB in RFC 1748, and it was separated from that document only because RFC 1748 had matured further in the standardisation process.

today: RFC 1749 is Historic, which means the RFC Editor recommends it for no further use. It was written as an incremental update to RFC 1748, the IEEE 802.5 Token Ring MIB, and has not itself been updated or obsoleted.

sections.title: What This MIB Covers
sections.content:
The memo defines a portion of the Management Information Base, the MIB, for use with network management protocols in the Internet community. In particular it describes managed objects used by IEEE 802.5 end stations for managing source routes on a Token Ring network where IEEE source routing is in use. IEEE source routing itself is described in the 802.5 Token Ring Access Method and Physical Layer Specifications and related ISO publications.

The memo is an incremental update to RFC 1748, the IEEE 802.5 MIB, which defines managed objects for interfaces to IEEE 802.5 Token Ring subnetworks. It is documented separately from RFC 1748 solely because of the latter's maturity within the Internet standardisation process.
sections.plainLanguage: This MIB covers one thing: the source routes that a Token Ring station has learned. It was split out from the wider 802.5 MIB only because that document had already been through more of the standardisation process.

sections.title: The SNMPv2 Network Management Framework
sections.content:
The SNMPv2 Network Management Framework has four major components. RFC 1442 defines the SMI, the mechanisms used for describing and naming objects for the purpose of management. STD 17, RFC 1213, defines MIB-II, the core set of managed objects for the Internet suite of protocols. RFC 1445 defines the administrative and other architectural aspects of the framework, and RFC 1448 defines the protocol used for network access to managed objects. The framework permits new objects to be defined for the purpose of experimentation and evaluation.

Managed objects are accessed through a virtual information store, the MIB. Objects in the MIB are defined using the subset of Abstract Syntax Notation One defined in the SMI. Each object type is named by an OBJECT IDENTIFIER, an administratively assigned name, and the object type together with an object instance serves to uniquely identify a specific instantiation of the object. For human convenience a textual string, termed the descriptor, is often used to refer to the object type.
sections.plainLanguage: The framework has four parts: a language for naming and describing managed objects, the core MIB of standard objects, the rules for who may do what, and the protocol used to reach the objects over the network. Each object has a numeric name, its object identifier, and an instance of that object stands for one particular value the manager can read or write.

sections.title: Source Routing on a Token Ring
sections.content:
Source routing extends the 802.5 protocol by assigning a unique ring number to each ring within the extended LAN, and a bridge number to each source routing bridge's connection to a ring. A Routing Information Field, the RIF, must be included in frames that need to traverse multiple rings. The RIF begins with a Routing Control field and is followed by up to eight Routing Descriptor fields.

The Routing Control field is two octets. Its first octet holds a three bit explorer indicator and a five bit length of the RIF field. Its second octet holds a one bit direction field, to use the routing descriptors in one direction or the other, and a maximum frame length subfield, whose length has recently been extended to six bits.

Each Routing Descriptor field is two octets as well. The first twelve bits carry the ring number and the last four bits carry the bridge number, so that a frame can be handed from bridge to bridge and ring to ring until it reaches the destination.
sections.plainLanguage: Source routing gives every ring in the network a number and every bridge connection a number. When a frame has to cross more than one ring, the sender writes down the route in a field at the front of the frame: first a control byte that says how to read the route, then one pair of bytes per hop, each holding the ring to go to and the bridge to go through.

sections.title: Relations to Other MIBs, Static Routes and Local Ring Destinations
sections.content:
RFC 1525 defines the MIB objects specific to source routing for source routing and SRT bridges, while this memo defines the MIB objects specific to source routing for source routing end stations. The two therefore cover opposite ends of the same mechanism.

The memo notes that it is unclear how many, if any, existing systems allow the creation or deletion of static 802.5 source routes by network management. SNMPv2 SMI defines the MAX-ACCESS clause as specifying the maximal level of access that makes protocol sense. The memo therefore provides support for static source routes through the dot5SrRouteStatus object, but the conformance statements allow for stations which do not support static source routes by requiring that compliant agents only need provide read access to dot5SrRouteStatus.

Entries should be included in the dot5SrRouteTable for destination MAC addresses which are on the same ring as the instrumented 802.5 interface. For such entries, dot5SrRouteDescr has the value of the zero-length string, and dot5SrRouteControl has the corresponding value.
sections.plainLanguage: Another document, RFC 1525, manages the bridges that carry source-routed frames; this one manages the stations at the ends. A station that cannot be told to create or delete routes only has to let a manager read the status of each row, and destinations on the station's own ring are listed with an empty route.

sections.title: The 802.5 Station Source Route Table
sections.content:
The module is named dot5SrMIB and is assigned the object identifier mib-2 42. It defines one table, dot5SrRouteTable, which contains the source routes known by an end station on an IEEE 802.5 Token Ring network in which IEEE source routing is in use, and which represents the 802.5 RIF database. Each row is a Dot5SrRouteEntry, indexed by ifIndex and dot5SrRouteDestination, where the ifIndex value refers to the value of MIB-II's ifIndex object for the interface on which the route is in effect.

An entry is created whenever a Single Path Explorer or an All Paths Explorer discovers a route to a neighbour not currently in the table, or whenever an All Paths Explorer discovers a better, for example shorter, route than the one currently stored. This is done on behalf of any network layer client.

The row holds four objects. dot5SrRouteDestination is the destination, of type MacAddress, and is not accessible. dot5SrRouteControl is the value of the Routing Control field for this route, an OCTET STRING of size 2, with read and create access. dot5SrRouteDescr is the embedded sequence of bridge and ring identifiers, of the textual convention SourceRoute, which is an OCTET STRING of size 0 to 30, again with read and create access, and holds the zero-length string for destinations on the local ring. dot5SrRouteStatus is the status of the row, of type RowStatus, with read and create access; the values of the other two objects can be modified while the row's status is active.

The conformance section makes write access optional. The dot5SrRouteStatus object need only support the value active, with a minimum access of read-only, and write access is not required for dot5SrRouteControl or dot5SrRouteDescr either. All three objects form the dot5SrRouteGroup object group, whose description reads: a collection of objects providing for the management of source routes in stations on IEEE 802.5 source-routing networks.
sections.plainLanguage: The table has one row for each destination the station knows how to reach. Each row holds the destination's hardware address, the two control bytes that say how to read the route, the route itself as a list of bridge and ring numbers, and a status saying whether the row is in use. A manager can read all of these, and can write the route fields, but only while the row is marked active.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The memo has a Security Considerations section, and its whole content is one sentence: security issues are not discussed in this memo.

Nothing in the document describes authentication, access control or confidentiality for the management information it defines. What it does say about who may touch the table is set out in the conformance statements, where write access to the route objects is not required of a compliant agent.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo does not discuss security. Its Security Considerations section says only that security issues are not discussed, so nothing in it should be read as a claim that the management objects are protected.

data.title: Routing Control field and Routing Descriptor field

viz.caption: THE FOUR OBJECTS IN EACH ROW OF THE ROUTE TABLE

items.title: dot5SrRouteDestination
items.text: The hardware address the route leads to. Read-only to the manager.

items.title: dot5SrRouteControl
items.text: The two bytes of the Routing Control field. Read and create.

items.title: dot5SrRouteDescr
items.text: The list of bridge and ring numbers, up to 30 bytes. Read and create.

items.title: dot5SrRouteStatus
items.text: Whether the row is in use. The other two objects may change only while it is active.
